title: Science Shorts
chapters: Air pressure: the weight of the sky

units.t: Science Shorts.
In this episode: Air pressure: the weight of the sky, Photosynthesis: how plants eat sunlight, Static electricity: sparks from nowhere and The secret life of soil.
Part one. Air pressure: the weight of the sky.
Right now the air is pressing on you with the weight of about ten tonnes on every square metre.
Here's why you don't notice, and how people first worked it out.
An ocean of air.
Air feels like nothing, but it is made of real molecules with real mass, and there are many kilometres of it stacked above your head.
At sea level, that weight presses on every surface with a force of roughly ten tonnes per square metre, about 101 kilopascals.
So why aren't we flattened?
Because air pressure pushes in every direction at once, not just downward, and the fluids and air inside your body push back outward with equal force.
Everything is balanced.
You only notice when that balance is suddenly upset, for example when your ears pop in a lift, or when a sealed packet of chips puffs up on a flight.
Torricelli's tube.
In the early 1600s, well diggers and engineers knew a frustrating fact.
Suction pumps could not raise water more than about ten metres, however well they were built.
Evangelista Torricelli, a former assistant to Galileo, suspected the weight of the air was the answer.
In 1643 he filled a long glass tube with mercury, which is about 13.
6 times denser than water, covered the open end and turned it upside down into a dish of mercury.
The column dropped until it stood about 76 centimetres high, leaving an empty space at the top.
The air pressing on the dish was holding the mercury up.
Torricelli had made the first barometer, and he noticed the height changed slightly from day to day.
Up the mountain.
The French thinker Blaise Pascal reasoned that if the atmosphere really had weight, less of it should press down at the top of a mountain.
In 1648 he persuaded his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, to test the idea on the Puy de Dôme, a volcanic peak in central France.
Périer left one mercury tube at the bottom with a watcher and carried another to the summit, about a kilometre higher.
At the top, the mercury column was several centimetres shorter.
Coming down, it rose again.
It was a beautifully simple experiment that settled the question.
Today the unit of pressure, the pascal, honours Pascal, and aircraft altimeters still work by measuring this same fall in pressure with height.
A push, not a pull.
Around 1650, Otto von Guericke, scientist and mayor of Magdeburg, built one of the first air pumps.
He fitted two copper hemispheres about half a metre across together with only a greased rim between them, then pumped out the air.
The atmosphere outside clamped the halves together.
Accounts describe two teams of horses failing to pull the sphere apart, yet when air was let back in, the halves simply fell open.
It is the same when you drink through a straw.
You lower the pressure inside your mouth, and the normal air pressure on the drink's surface pushes it up.
Suction cups work the same way.
That also explains the old pump puzzle: the atmosphere can push water up only about ten metres, because that is the height of water column it can balance.
Pressure in daily life.
Air pressure changes from place to place, and those differences drive the weather.
High pressure usually brings sinking air and settled, clear skies, while low pressure brings rising air, cloud and often rain.
Wind is air moving from higher pressure towards lower, which is why the curved lines on a weather map, called isobars, are so useful.
Pressure also changes how we cook.
A pressure cooker traps steam, raising the pressure so water boils at around 120°C and food cooks much faster.
And at an airliner's cruising height, the outside air is far too thin to breathe for long, so cabins are pressurised to a level similar to being on a mountain a couple of kilometres high.
The key idea: Air has weight, and the atmosphere presses on everything, but we are not crushed because the pressure is balanced.
Part two. Photosynthesis: how plants eat sunlight.
A towering gum tree is built mostly from thin air, and the process that does it also made the oxygen you are breathing.
Built from thin air.
In the 1600s, the Flemish scientist Jan Baptist van Helmont planted a small willow in carefully weighed, dried soil and gave it nothing but water for five years.
The willow gained a great deal of weight, yet the soil had barely changed.
He concluded the tree was made from water.
He was partly right, but he missed the most surprising ingredient.
Most of a plant's dry mass is carbon, and that carbon comes from carbon dioxide drawn out of the air.
A huge gum tree is, in a very real sense, built from thin air, stitched together with water and powered by sunlight.
The process that does this is called photosynthesis.
The basic recipe.
A plant draws water up from its roots and takes in carbon dioxide through tiny leaf pores called stomata.
Using the energy in sunlight, it rearranges these into glucose, a sugar, and releases oxygen.
In shorthand, six carbon dioxide plus six water become one glucose and six oxygen.
Glucose is the plant's food and building material: burned for energy, stored as starch, or linked into cellulose for cell walls and wood.
Almost every food you eat traces back to this reaction.
It seems natural that the oxygen comes from the carbon dioxide.
But 1940s experiments with a traceable heavy oxygen showed it comes from water, which plants rip apart using light.
Plants do this at ordinary temperatures, and researchers are still trying to copy it to make clean fuels such as hydrogen.
Why leaves are green.
The green of leaves comes from chlorophyll, a pigment packed inside structures called chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll is very good at absorbing red and blue light, which powers photosynthesis.
It is poor at absorbing green, so much of that light bounces back towards our eyes.
Leaves also contain yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids.
In many deciduous trees, autumn reveals them.
As days shorten, the tree stops making chlorophyll and breaks down what it has, and the hidden yellows and oranges show through.
Red autumn colours are different: they often come from new pigments made in the leaf at that time of year.
Most Australian native trees, including eucalypts, are evergreen, so our famous autumn displays usually come from introduced species.
Two stages, many tricks.
Photosynthesis has two linked stages in the chloroplast.
First, chlorophyll absorbs light, splits water, releases oxygen and charges two energy-carrying molecules, ATP and NADPH, like freshly charged batteries.
Second, in the Calvin cycle, those batteries power the building of sugar.
An enzyme called RuBisCO grabs carbon dioxide from the air and fixes it into an organic molecule.
RuBisCO is slow and sometimes grabs oxygen by mistake, so plants make vast amounts of it.
It is probably the most abundant protein on Earth.
Opening stomata lets water escape, a problem in hot, dry places.
Sugarcane, maize and Australia's spinifex grasses use C4 photosynthesis, concentrating carbon dioxide around RuBisCO.
Cacti, pineapples and many succulents use CAM, opening their stomata only at night, storing carbon dioxide as an acid and using it by day with pores shut.
A planet remade.
Photosynthesis is far older than plants.
Microbes developed it first, and one group, the cyanobacteria, worked out how to split water and release oxygen.
Over hundreds of millions of years that oxygen built up, and around 2.
4 billion years ago the atmosphere changed dramatically in the Great Oxidation Event.
Some early oxygen reacted with iron dissolved in the oceans, helping to form banded iron formations.
Western Australia's Pilbara holds spectacular examples, and they supply much of the iron ore the country exports.
Today, tiny ocean plankton are thought to produce around half of the world's oxygen, with land plants providing much of the rest.
Even the coal, oil and gas we burn are stored sunlight, captured by photosynthesis millions of years ago.
The key idea: A tree's mass comes mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.
Part three. Static electricity: sparks from nowhere.
That zap from a car door or a supermarket trolley is the same force that gave electricity its name, and it runs the printer in your office.
Amber and a word.
Ancient Greeks noticed that amber, the golden fossilised tree resin, attracted bits of straw, feathers and dust when rubbed with fur or wool.
Tradition credits the philosopher Thales of Miletus, around 600 BC, with describing this, though nothing he wrote survives.
The Greek word for amber was elektron.
Almost two thousand years later, in 1600, the English physician William Gilbert showed in a book on magnetism that many other materials, like glass and sulfur, behaved the same way.
He called them electricus, Latin for like amber.
From that root came the word electricity, so every power point in your home carries an echo of a lump of ancient resin.
Where the charge comes from.
Atoms contain positive protons and negative electrons, normally in balance.
When two different materials touch and rub, electrons can transfer from one to the other.
The one that gains electrons becomes negative and the other positive.
Scientists rank materials by this tendency in the triboelectric series.
Opposite charges attract and like charges repel.
Rub a balloon on your jumper and it sticks to a wall, even though the wall is neutral.
The negative balloon pushes electrons in the wall's surface slightly away and draws positive charge closer, and the nearer attraction wins.
This is induction.
Put your hand on a Van de Graaff generator and your hairs all share one charge, repel and stand up.
Physicists still don't fully understand how charge moves in contact.
Why you get zapped.
Walking across carpet in rubber-soled shoes, or sliding across a car seat, can build up several thousand volts on your body.
Nothing happens until you reach for something metal, like a door handle.
Then the charge jumps the gap in a tiny spark, and you feel the zap.
Despite the high voltage, the shock is harmless because the amount of charge is tiny and the current lasts a fraction of a second.
Shocks are far more common in dry conditions, such as cold winter days or air-conditioned offices.
In humid air, a thin film of moisture lets charge leak away before it can build up.
A simple trick is to touch metal with a key first, so the spark jumps from the key.
Static at work.
In 1938, American patent lawyer Chester Carlson, tired of copying documents by hand, made the first dry copy using static electricity in a makeshift lab in Queens, New York.
His process, later called xerography, took years to find a backer but became the basis of the photocopier and the laser printer.
Inside, light creates a pattern of charge on a drum, powdery toner sticks only to the charged areas, and heat fuses it onto paper.
Static also cleans the air.
Electrostatic precipitators, developed in the early twentieth century, charge smoke particles in chimneys so they are drawn onto collecting plates.
Car makers use the same idea to spray paint evenly onto charged car bodies.
When static is dangerous.
Most shocks are merely annoying, but a spark in the wrong place can start a fire.
Petrol gives off flammable vapour, and fuel stations warn people not to get back into their car while refuelling, because sliding across the seat can build up charge that may spark at the nozzle.
Touching the metal body of the car before handling the nozzle helps discharge you safely.
If a fire starts, move away and call 000.
Fine dust from flour, sugar or grain can explode if a spark ignites a dense cloud of it, which is why factories and silos manage static carefully.
Electronics are vulnerable too.
A discharge too small for you to feel can still damage a microchip, so technicians often wear grounding wrist straps.
The key idea: The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber, which attracts small objects when rubbed.
Part four. The secret life of soil.
The ground beneath your feet is not dirt: it is a living, breathing system that took thousands of years to build and feeds almost everything on land.
A crowded handful.
A handful of healthy soil is one of the most crowded habitats on Earth.
Soil scientists note that a single teaspoon of rich soil can hold hundreds of millions to billions of microorganisms.
Bacteria, fungi, single-celled protists and microscopic nematode worms share the space with mites, springtails, beetle larvae, ants and earthworms.
Most of these organisms have never been studied, and many have not been named.
The earthy smell after rain comes partly from geosmin, a compound made by certain soil bacteria.
People are remarkably sensitive to it.
Far from lifeless dirt, soil is a busy underground city where life is recycled day and night.
Slow to build.
Soil begins as rock.
Heat and cold, freezing water, plant roots and rainwater slowly break it apart.
Lichens and mosses colonise the surface and add organic material as they die.
Microbes and small animals mix it with mineral grains, and layers form: dark, humus-rich soil near the top, paler mineral layers below, then the parent rock.
This is extremely slow.
A few centimetres of new soil can take hundreds of years or more, so soil lost to erosion is effectively lost for good.
In the 1930s, drought and poor farming on the American Great Plains caused the Dust Bowl, when dust storms stripped away topsoil and forced many families off their farms.
Soil is also estimated to hold more carbon than the atmosphere and all living plants combined.
Sand, silt and clay.
The mineral part of soil comes in three particle sizes.
Sand is the largest and feels gritty.
Silt is finer and smooth, a bit like flour.
Clay is tiny and sticky when wet.
Their balance gives a soil its texture, and texture matters enormously.
Sandy soil drains fast and warms quickly but holds little water or nutrients.
Clay holds plenty of both but can become waterlogged, and sets hard when dry.
Gardeners prize loam, a mix of all three, which holds moisture while still letting air reach the roots.
A simple test: roll a moist pinch between your fingers.
Clay forms a ribbon, and sand falls apart.
Fungi and worms at work.
Most land plants partner with fungi in relationships called mycorrhizae.
The plant supplies sugars from photosynthesis.
In return, fungal threads called hyphae spread far beyond the roots and bring back water and nutrients, especially phosphorus.
The partnership is ancient and may have helped the first plants colonise land.
Claims that forests share food and warnings through a 'wood wide web' are debated, so treat them with caution.
Earthworms swallow soil and decaying matter, leave nutrient-rich castings, and open tunnels for air and water.
Darwin devoted his last book, in 1881, to them.
Bacteria and fungi break dead material into substances plants can absorb again.
Victoria's giant Gippsland earthworm can reach about a metre long.
Australia's ancient soils.
Australia's soils are often very old and very poor.
Much of the land has been stable for a long time, without recent glaciers grinding up fresh rock or widespread volcanoes spreading mineral-rich ash.
Over millions of years, rain has leached out many nutrients, and phosphorus is often scarce.
Native plants have adapted.
Banksias, grevilleas and their relatives grow dense mats of fine cluster roots that release chemicals to free up tightly bound phosphorus.
Some natives are even harmed by the phosphorus in ordinary garden fertiliser.
Farmers have long added fertilisers such as superphosphate, and scientists study how to farm these soils without degrading them or causing salinity.
Serious erosion and dust storms have happened here too.
The community Landcare movement began in Victoria in the late 1980s and now has thousands of local groups repairing land.
The key idea: Healthy soil teems with life, from bacteria and fungi to worms and insects.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why aren't we crushed by the weight of the atmosphere?
Answer. Air pushes all ways and we push back.
Question two. Where does most of a tree's dry mass come from?
Answer. Carbon dioxide from the air.
Question three. Where does the word electricity come from?
Answer. The Greek word for amber.
Question four. Why does the ground smell earthy after rain?
Answer. Soil bacteria make geosmin, a compound people detect.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
